lesson.title: Dutch Idioms & Directness
lesson.subtitle: lekker, gezellig, doe normaal, graag — the words that make Dutch sound Dutch

hook.title: Small Words, Big Culture
hook.content: Lekker, gezellig, graag, zin hebben: these little words carry much of Dutch social life. They are not decoration; they are how Dutch frames pleasure, company and desire.

pattern.title: Zin and trek are things you have
pattern.content: Ik heb zin in koffie ('I feel like coffee'), ik heb trek in brood ('I feel like bread'). Pleasure and appetite are possessed with hebben. Gezellig describes shared warmth; lekker extends from taste to almost anything pleasant.
pattern.linguist_note: Zin and trek are native Dutch nouns whose meanings widen into modal-like desire; English uses 'feel like' instead.
pattern.trap_note: Zin hebben in is not 'to have sense in'. It is the everyday way to say you feel like something.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Dutch Idioms & Directness):
exercises.target_answer: lekker, gezellig, graag, de zin, de trek, doen
exercises.meaning: tasty; nice, cosy, convivial, gladly; please, sense; desire; sentence, appetite; pull, to do
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Dutch Idioms & Directness": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “I feel like coffee.”?
exercises.explanation: “Ik heb zin in koffie.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Dutch Idioms & Directness”.

cues: The pattern: Zin and trek are things you have
It means: I feel like bread.
exercises.explanation: “Ik heb trek in brood.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Zin and trek are things you have.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Zin hebben in is not 'to have sense in'. It is the everyday way to say you feel like something.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Het is gezellig.” is word-for-word “It is companion-like.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Zin and trek are things you have.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Doe normaal.” reuses only material taught in “Dutch Idioms & Directness” — Zin and trek are things you have.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Doe normaal.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Zin and trek are things you have.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I like eating fish.”
twist.explanation: Graag marks liking: 'I eat fish gladly' is the Dutch way to say you like it.

summary.outcome: Use zin hebben, trek hebben, gezellig and graag in everyday sentences.
summary.takeaway: Dutch often expresses desire and pleasure with small possessed nouns and adverbs, not with 'like'.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Idiom Gym.

lekker.etymology_derivation: From an old sense of lekken ('lick'); Dutch extends it to weather and sleep.

gezellig.etymology_derivation: From gezel ('companion'); it describes shared warmth, not just a room.

graag.etymology_derivation: The adverb of willingness; Dutch uses it where English says 'like to'.

zin.etymology_derivation: English sense is a Latin loan; Dutch zin is the native word for sense/desire.

trek.etymology_derivation: From trekken ('pull'); appetite is a pull toward food.

doen.etymology_derivation: English do and Dutch doen are the same verb, spelled with oe for /u/.
